text: With $E(x)$: $x$ is an engineer and $K(x)$: $x$ knows Python, which formula says **“every engineer knows Python”**?
solution: “Every engineer” is a universal over a restricted noun, so the restriction becomes the hypothesis of $\to$.
$\forall x\, (E(x) \to K(x))$: for each $x$, if $x$ is an engineer then $x$ knows Python.
Non-engineers keep the promise vacuously, exactly as the English intends.
concept: ∀ pairs with →.

common_wrong.why: $\forall x\, (E \wedge K)$ claims everyone is an engineer who knows Python.
That is “some engineer knows Python”.
$\exists x\, (E \to K)$ is true as soon as one non-engineer exists.

text: With $F(x)$: $x$ is a fruit and $S(x)$: $x$ is sour, which formula says **“some fruit is sour”**?
solution: “Some fruit” is an existential over a restricted noun: the restriction is joined with $\wedge$.
$\exists x\, (F(x) \wedge S(x))$: one object that is a fruit and sour, both at once.
concept: ∃ pairs with ∧.

common_wrong.why: $\exists x\, (F \to S)$ is made true by any non-fruit.
That is “every fruit is sour”.
$\forall x\, (F \wedge S)$ says everything is a sour fruit.

text: The domain is $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ and $y \mid x$ means $y$ divides $x$. For how many $x$ in the domain is $\exists y\, (y \mid x \wedge 1 < y \wedge y < x)$ true?
solution: The formula says $x$ has a divisor strictly between 1 and $x$, i.e. $x$ is composite (with the divisor inside the domain).
1, 2, 3 and 5 have no such divisor. 4 has $y = 2$; 6 has $y = 2$ (and 3).
So the formula is true for $x = 4$ and $x = 6$.
concept: Read a number-theory formula back into its textbook meaning, then test each element.

common_wrong.why: Counting 1 as composite: 1 has no divisor strictly between 1 and 1.
Counting the primes instead of the composites.

text: Which formulas are equivalent to $\neg\forall x\, (P(x) \to Q(x))$? (Select all that apply.)
solution: Push the negation through: $\neg\forall x\, \varphi \equiv \exists x\, \neg\varphi$.

$
eg(P 	o Q) \equiv P \wedge 
eg Q$, so the formula is $\exists x\, (P(x) \wedge 
eg Q(x))$: option A.

Option C: $P 	o Q \equiv 
eg P \vee Q$, so $\exists x\, 
eg(
eg P(x) \vee Q(x))$ is the same formula.
B and D keep a $\forall$: they are much stronger claims.

common_wrong.why: Keeps $\forall$ and negates only the conclusion: “no $P$ is a $Q$”.
$\forall x\, (\neg P \vee \neg Q)$ is “nothing is both $P$ and $Q$”.

text: Which is the negation of $\forall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = 0)$?
solution: Flip each quantifier, keeping the order $x, y$: $\exists x\, \forall y$.
Negate the matrix: $x + y \ne 0$.
Result: $\exists x\, \forall y\, (x + y \ne 0)$.
concept: Negation flips every quantifier and keeps their order.

common_wrong.why: Flips the order of the variables as well; the order never changes.
Flips the quantifiers but leaves the matrix un-negated.
Negates only the matrix.

text: On the domain $\{a, b, c\}$, $R$ holds exactly for $(a, a), (a, b), (a, c), (b, c), (c, c)$. How many of these six sentences are true: $\forall x \forall y R$, $\exists x \exists y R$, $\forall x \exists y R$, $\exists x \forall y R$, $\forall y \exists x R$, $\exists y \forall x R$ (each with matrix $R(x, y)$)?
solution: Draw the grid: row $a$ is T T T, row $b$ is F F T, row $c$ is F F T.
$\forall\forall$: F (cell $(b, a)$). $\exists\exists$: T. $\forall x \exists y$: every row has a T: T. $\exists x \forall y$: row $a$ is full: T.
$\forall y \exists x$: every column has a T (row $a$ is full): T. $\exists y \forall x$: column $c$ is full: T.
Five of the six are true.
concept: Read ∀x∃y along rows, ∃x∀y as a full row, ∀y∃x along columns, ∃y∀x as a full column.

common_wrong.why: Missing that column $c$ is full, so $\exists y\, \forall x$ is true.
Forgetting that $\forall\forall$ needs every cell.

text: With $G(x)$: $x$ is a graduate and $E(x)$: $x$ is eligible, which formula says **“only graduates are eligible”**?
solution: “Only graduates” restricts who can be eligible: anyone eligible must be a graduate.
So: for every $x$, if $x$ is eligible then $x$ is a graduate, $\forall x\, (E(x) \to G(x))$.
concept: “Only A are B” = ∀x (B → A): the arrow reverses.

common_wrong.why: That is “all graduates are eligible”, a different claim.
That only says some eligible graduate exists.
Says everyone is an eligible graduate.

text: Which formulas say that **exactly one** element has property $P$? (Select all that apply.)

options.t: $\exists x\, P(x) \wedge \forall x\, \forall y\, ((P(x) \wedge P(y)) \to x = y)$

solution: Option A is the standard form: some $x$ has $P$, and every $y$ with $P$ equals $x$.
Option B is “at least one” ∧ “at most one”, the same meaning.
Option C alone is true when **no** element has $P$; option D says at least two.
concept: Exactly one = at least one + at most one.

common_wrong.why: “At most one”: it is true when nothing has $P$.
That is “at least two”.

text: Over the integers $\mathbb{Z}$, which sentence is **true**?
solution: B: for any $x$, take $y = x - 1$; then $y < x$. True.
A: any candidate $y$ fails at $x = y$. C: any candidate $x$ fails at $y = x - 1$. D fails at $y = x$.
concept: ∀∃ lets the witness depend on x; ∃∀ needs one witness for all.

common_wrong.why: No integer exceeds every integer (it fails against itself).
$\mathbb{Z}$ has no least element; on $\mathbb{N}$ this would be true.
Fails when $x = y$.

text: On the domain $\{1, 2, 3\}$ with the usual $>$, for how many of the $2^3$ choices of a unary predicate $P$ is $\forall x\, (P(x) \to \exists y\, (y > x \wedge P(y)))$ true?
solution: The sentence says: every element of $P$ has a larger element of $P$.
If $P$ is non-empty, its largest element $m$ needs some $y > m$ in $P$, which is impossible.
So only $P = \varnothing$ works (vacuously). Answer: 1.
concept: A finite non-empty set has a largest element; ‘always a bigger one’ forces emptiness (or an infinite domain).

common_wrong.why: Counting $P = \{1, 2, 3\}$, but its largest element 3 has nothing above it.
Forgetting that the empty predicate makes a ∀x (P(x) → …) vacuously true.

text: Which formula is **valid**?

options.t: $\forall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)) \to (\forall x\, P(x) \vee \forall x\, Q(x))$
$(\exists x\, P(x) \wedge \exists x\, Q(x)) \to \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x))$
$(\forall x\, P(x) \to \forall x\, Q(x)) \to \forall x\, (P(x) \to Q(x))$

solution: C: if $P \wedge Q$ holds for every $x$, then in particular $P$ holds for every $x$ (∀ distributes over ∧).
A and B are the wrong directions of the one-way laws; D is the converse of a one-way law.
The turn-taking world $D = \{1, 2\}$, $P = \{1\}$, $Q = \{2\}$ refutes A and B; $P = \{1\}$, $Q = \varnothing$ refutes D.
concept: ∀ distributes over ∧; ∀ over ∨ and ∃ over ∧ only go one way.

common_wrong.why: ∀ over ∨: fails when P and Q take turns.
Two witnesses need not be one.
When $\forall x\, P$ is false the hypothesis is vacuous, yet $P \to Q$ can fail at one element.

text: Classify $\exists x\, P(x) \wedge \exists x\, \neg P(x)$.
solution: It is true on $D = \{1, 2\}$ with $P = \{1\}$ (witnesses 1 and 2): satisfiable.
It is false on any world where $P$ holds everywhere: not valid.
So it is satisfiable but not valid (contingent).
concept: Satisfiable = some world; valid = every world.

common_wrong.why: A world where P holds everywhere makes it false.
The world {1, 2} with P = {1} satisfies it.
No formula is both valid and unsatisfiable on a non-empty domain.

text: On the domain $\{1, 2\}$, unary predicates $P$ and $Q$ can be chosen in $4 \times 4 = 16$ ways. In how many of these worlds is $\forall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)) \to (\forall x\, P(x) \vee \forall x\, Q(x))$ **false**?
solution: The implication is false when $\forall x\, (P \vee Q)$ is true and both $\forall x\, P$ and $\forall x\, Q$ are false.
That forces $\{P, Q\} = \{\{1\}, \{2\}\}$ in either order: 2 worlds.
concept: Count counter-models by translating ‘false’ into conditions on the sets.

common_wrong.why: Forgetting the mirror world P = {2}, Q = {1}.
Also counting worlds where P or Q is all of {1, 2}, which make the conclusion true.

text: $W$ is a sentence with no free $x$. Which formulas are equivalent to $\forall x\, (P(x) \to W)$? (Select all that apply.)
solution: $P(x) \to W \equiv \neg P(x) \vee W$, so C is the same formula.
Pull $\forall x$ past $W$: $\forall x\, \neg P(x) \vee W \equiv \neg\exists x\, P(x) \vee W \equiv \exists x\, P(x) \to W$: A.

D: $
eg\exists x\, (P(x) \wedge 
eg W) \equiv  orall x\, 
eg(P(x) \wedge 
eg W) \equiv  orall x\, (P(x) 	o W)$.
B has $\forall$ where $\exists$ is needed.
concept: A quantifier leaving a hypothesis flips.

common_wrong.why: The classic wrong pull-out (GATE 2020): it is much weaker.

text: Which is a prenex form of $\exists x\, P(x) \to \forall y\, Q(y)$?
solution: $\exists x$ sits in the hypothesis: pulling it out flips it to $\forall x$.
$\forall y$ sits in the conclusion: it comes out unchanged.
Result: $\forall x\, \forall y\, (P(x) \to Q(y))$.
concept: Hypothesis quantifiers flip; conclusion quantifiers do not.

common_wrong.why: Keeps ∃x although it left a hypothesis.
Flips both quantifiers.
Flips the wrong one.

text:
What is the size of the smallest model of $\exists x\, \exists y\, \exists z\, (x 
e y \wedge y 
e z \wedge x 
e z)$?
solution: The sentence asks for three pairwise different elements.
A domain with 3 elements works; 2 cannot (two of $x, y, z$ would be equal).
concept: Equality lets a sentence demand ‘at least n’ elements.

common_wrong.why: With two elements, two of the three witnesses must coincide.
Forgetting that ≠ forces different elements.

text: Which sentence has models, but **only infinite** ones?

options.t: $\forall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) \wedge \forall x\, \neg R(x, x)$
$\forall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) \wedge \forall x\, \neg R(x, x) \wedge \forall x\, \forall y\, \forall z\, ((R(x, y) \wedge R(y, z)) \to R(x, z))$

solution: A and B have finite models: a 2-cycle $R = \{(1, 2), (2, 1)\}$ satisfies both.
C adds transitivity: every chain of successors must be new forever (a cycle would give $R(x, x)$), so no finite model; $(\mathbb{N}, <)$ is a model.
D has the one-element model with $R = \{(1, 1)\}$.
concept: Serial + transitive + irreflexive forces an infinite chain.

common_wrong.why: $R = \{(1, 1)\}$ is a one-element model.
The 2-cycle on {1, 2} is a model.
$R(1, 1)$ on {1} is a model.

text: Which sentences are logically implied by $\exists y\, \forall x\, R(x, y)$? (Select all that apply.)
solution: A: ∃∀ implies ∀∃: the single y works for every x.
B: the domain is non-empty, so some pair is related.
C: rows and columns: ‘every y is hit’ does not follow from ‘some column is full’.
D: a full column is not a full grid.
concept: ∃y∀x ⇒ ∀x∃y; ∃∀ says nothing about the other columns.

common_wrong.why: $D = \{1, 2\}$, $R = \{(1, 1), (2, 1)\}$: column 1 is full but column 2 is empty.
The same world: $R(1, 2)$ is false.

text: Which formula is **NOT** valid?

options.t: $\forall x\, (P(x) \to Q(x)) \to (\exists x\, P(x) \to \exists x\, Q(x))$
$(\exists x\, P(x) \to \exists x\, Q(x)) \to \forall x\, (P(x) \to Q(x))$

solution: A is valid on non-empty domains; B and C are rows of the one-way table.
D is the converse of C: with $P = \{1\}$, $Q = \{2\}$ on $\{1, 2\}$, $\exists x\, P \to \exists x\, Q$ is true but $P(1) \to Q(1)$ is false.
concept: One-way laws: the converse of a valid law is the usual NOT-valid option.

common_wrong.why: Valid: the non-empty domain supplies a witness.
Valid: the witness of P ∧ Q is a witness of P.
Valid: apply the promise to the witness of P.

text: How many of these five are valid? (i) $\forall x\, \forall y\, R(x, y) \to \forall x\, R(x, x)$; (ii) $\forall x\, R(x, x) \to \forall x\, \forall y\, R(x, y)$; (iii) $\exists x\, \forall y\, R(x, y) \to \forall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y)$; (iv) $\forall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) \to \exists y\, \forall x\, R(x, y)$; (v) $\exists x\, (P(x) \to \forall y\, P(y))$.
solution: (i) valid (instantiate $y = x$); (ii) not valid (a reflexive relation need not relate every pair).
(iii) valid: the row $x$ that is full gives every column $y$ a T. (iv) not valid (Lesson 1's grid).
(v) valid (the ‘drinker’ sentence): if $P$ holds everywhere, any $x$ works; if not, pick an $x$ with $\neg P(x)$, which makes $P(x) \to \dots$ vacuously true.
Total: 3.
concept: Prove the valid ones by take–unpack–build; refute the rest with small worlds.

common_wrong.why: Missing (v): it looks paradoxical but is valid on non-empty domains.
Thinking (iv) holds: ∀∃ does not give ∃∀.
